title: Hebrew and Prayer
subtitle: Letters, vowels, the Shema, the Amidah and blessings
intro: Here you will learn to read Hebrew letters and vowels, and get to know the main prayers — the Shema and the Amidah — the basic blessings and the objects a Jew prays with. This is enough to follow a synagogue service with confidence and to answer the beit din's questions about prayer.

overview.why: Hebrew is the language of the Torah and of prayer, and prayer itself accompanies a Jew from waking until sleep. This section gives the essential minimum: reading letters and vowels, the meaning of the Shema and the Amidah, blessings and the objects of prayer. With this material, prayer stops being someone else's text and becomes personal.
overview.examFocus: At the beit din you will almost certainly be asked to say the first line of the Shema and explain it, to name the daily prayers and the blessings over food, and to talk about tefillin, the tallit, the kippah and the mezuzah. A candidate is usually not expected to be fluent in the language — what is expected is the ability to read the prayers slowly, knowledge of key words and an understanding of how prayer is built into their everyday life.
goals: Read Hebrew letters and vowels, putting words together syllable by syllable
Say the Shema and the basic brachot in Hebrew and understand how the Amidah is structured
Know the three daily prayers, the minyan and how a synagogue is arranged
Bless food and the morning, and know when “Shehecheyanu” is said
Talk about the tallit, tefillin, kippah and mezuzah as is customary in your own community

deeper.title: A siddur with translation as a textbook
deeper.text: Open your community's siddur to the Shema and the Amidah. For study with a Russian translation, the siddur “Vrata Molitvy” (“Gates of Prayer”) is convenient: read the Hebrew aloud syllable by syllable and check each line against the translation until these prayers become familiar.

deeper.title: The halacha of the Shema and the Amidah
deeper.text: Chapters 17–18 of the Kitzur Shulchan Aruch discuss in detail the time and order of reciting the Shema and the laws of the Amidah — check your practice against them if you are preparing along the Orthodox line.

deeper.title: Prayer as a way of life
deeper.text: In R. Donin's book “To Be a Jew,” read the chapters on daily prayer and blessings: the book helps you sense how prayer enters a Jew's ordinary day.

deeper.title: Pirkei Avot on prayer
deeper.text: In the second chapter of tractate Avot, read the words of Rabbi Shimon (2:13): “Be careful with the reading of the Shema and with prayer. And when you pray, do not make your prayer a fixed routine, but a plea for mercy before the Omnipresent.” This thought is a key to prayer.

deeper.title: Prayer in Progressive communities
deeper.text: On the website of the giyur school of the “Shaarei Shalom” community, see how a Progressive community speaks about prayer: this helps you understand its practice from the inside. The siddur of this movement is “Mishkan T'filah.”

deeper.title: The Mishkan T'filah siddur and Progressive prayer
deeper.text: Mishkan T'filah (CCAR Press, 2007) is the main siddur of the North American Reform movement: Hebrew and translation side by side, the names of the matriarchs in the Amidah, different versions of some blessings, room for prayer in an understandable language. Compare its structure with Nusach Ashkenaz after the lesson on the siddur. Russian-speaking Progressive communities may also use other siddurim — ask at your synagogue.

lessons.title: The alphabet: twenty-two letters
keyIdeas: Hebrew is the language of the Torah and of prayer; the beit din usually does not require fluency, but expects the ability to read the prayers slowly and knowledge of key words.
The alphabet has 22 consonant letters, is read from right to left and has no capital letters; five letters have final forms (sofit).
A dot inside a letter is a dagesh: with it the sound is a stop (“b”, “k”, “p”), without it “v”, “ch”, “f”; shin has its dot on top: on the right it is “sh”, on the left “s”.

Alef is a “silent” letter: only the vowel under it is read; in modern Hebrew ayin is almost silent, like alef (in the Eastern communities it is a guttural sound); hey is a light breath and is usually not sounded at the end of a word.
Every letter has a numerical value (gematria); the word “chai” (“alive”) adds up to 18, which is why gifts for celebrations are given in multiples of 18.

blocks.text: Hebrew is the language of the Torah, of prayer and of most of the Jewish tradition. Even if you pray from a siddur with a Russian translation, being able to read Hebrew letters opens the text itself to you: you will be able to follow the cantor, find the right place in the siddur and recognize the words heard in the synagogue every day. The beit din usually does not require a candidate to be fluent in the language, but it does expect you to be able to read the prayers, at least slowly, and to know the key words. It all begins with the alphabet — the **alef-bet**.
the Hebrew alphabet; named after its first two letters, just like the Greek “alpha-beta”
The main features of the script

items: The alphabet has **22 letters**, and all of them stand for consonants. Vowels are shown by separate marks — the vowel signs (nekudot), which are the subject of the next lesson.
Hebrew is written and read **from right to left**. Books, including the siddur, open from the side that seems to a Russian reader to be the “end”.
There are no capital letters. Instead, five letters have a special **final form**, used only at the end of a word.
The printed “square” script (ktav ashuri) is used in the Torah, the siddur and books. For everyday handwriting there is a cursive script whose letters look different.
Every letter has a numerical value. This is the basis of **gematria** — a traditional method of interpretation through numbers.

blocks.text: The first group: from alef to vav

blocks.he: א ב ג ד ה ו
blocks.translit: alef, bet (vet), gimel, dalet, hey, vav
blocks.ru: Alef is a “silent” letter: it has no sound of its own and serves as a carrier for a vowel. Bet is “b” (with a dot inside) or “v” (without a dot). Gimel is “g”. Dalet is “d”. Hey is a light breath, like the English h (usually not pronounced at the end of a word). Vav is “v”; it also serves to mark the vowels “o” and “u”.

blocks.text: Pay attention to **alef** (א): beginners often try to “pronounce” it, but it has no sound — only the vowel under it is read. So the word אָמֵן is read “amen”. In Russian transcription the letter **hey** (ה) often disappears altogether or is rendered as “a”: hence spellings like “Rosh a-Shana” and “a-motzi”, although in Hebrew a light h is heard there.
The second group: from zayin to lamed

blocks.he: ז ח ט י כ ל
blocks.translit: zayin, chet, tet, yud, kaf (chaf), lamed
blocks.ru: Zayin is “z”. Chet is a guttural “ch”, pronounced deeper in the throat than the Russian “kh”. Tet is “t”. Yud is “y”; it also indicates the vowels “i” and “e”. Kaf is “k” (with a dot) or “ch” (without a dot). Lamed is “l”, the only letter that rises above the line.

blocks.text: **Yud** is the smallest letter of the alphabet, almost a dot; the word יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yisrael) begins with it, and the tradition often calls it a symbol of humility. **Lamed**, by contrast, is the tallest. In modern Israeli pronunciation the sounds of **chet** (ח) and **chaf** (כ without a dot) are almost identical, but among people from the Eastern communities chet sounds noticeably deeper, from the throat.
The third group: from mem to tzadi

blocks.he: מ נ ס ע פ צ
blocks.translit: mem, nun, samech, ayin, pey (fey), tzadi
blocks.ru: Mem is “m”. Nun is “n”. Samech is “s”. Ayin is almost silent in modern Hebrew, like alef (in the Eastern communities it is a special guttural sound). Pey is “p” (with a dot) or “f” (without a dot). Tzadi is “tz”.

blocks.text: The fourth group: from kuf to tav

blocks.ru: Kuf is “k”. Reish is “r” (in Israeli pronunciation it is guttural, as in French). Shin is “sh” (dot over the right prong). Sin is “s” (dot over the left prong). Tav is “t”.

blocks.text: In Hebrew the sounds “k”, “t”, “s”, “v” and “ch” can each be written with two different letters: “k” with both כּ and ק; “t” with both ט and ת; “s” with both ס and שׂ; “v” with both ב and ו; “ch” with both ח and כ. In ancient times these letters sounded different, but today the difference survives mainly in spelling. So when you hear a word, you cannot always tell right away how it is spelled — the spelling has to be memorized.
Final forms: ך ם ן ף ץ

blocks.he: כ → ך · מ → ם · נ → ן · פ → ף · צ → ץ
blocks.translit: kaf sofit, mem sofit, nun sofit, pey (fey) sofit, tzadi sofit
blocks.ru: Five letters change their shape at the end of a word. The sound stays the same; only the written form changes: in four of them the tail drops below the line, and final mem becomes a closed square.

blocks.text: The word **sofit** (סוֹפִית) means “final”. The traditional mnemonic word for remembering these five letters is **“MaNTzePaCh”** (מנצפ״ך). Examples from the prayers: in the word בָּרוּךְ (“blessed”) the last letter is final chaf ך; in the word שָׁלוֹם (“peace”) it is final mem ם; in the word אָמֵן it is final nun ן. Final chaf is almost always written with two small dots inside (this is the shva sign), while a final kaf with a dot is extremely rare.
“Twin” letters: with a dot and without

blocks.he: בּ / ב · כּ / כ · פּ / פ · שׁ / שׂ
blocks.translit: bet / vet · kaf / chaf · pey / fey · shin / sin
blocks.ru: A dot inside a letter (dagesh) makes the sound “hard”, a stop: “b”, “k”, “p”. Without it the sound becomes fricative: “v”, “ch”, “f”. On the letter ש the dot is placed on top: on the right it is “sh”, on the left “s”.

blocks.text: The dot inside a letter is called a **dagesh** (דָּגֵשׁ). At the beginning of a word the letters bet, kaf and pey are usually written with a dagesh: בָּרוּךְ — “baruch”, כֹּהֵן — “kohen”, פֶּסַח — “Pesach”. In the middle and at the end of a word, after a vowel, there is often no dagesh and the sound softens: think of the word מֶלֶךְ — “melech”, “king”, where the final letter is read as “ch”.

In Ashkenazi pronunciation, which you will hear in many synagogues of the diaspora, the letter tav without a dagesh (ת) is read as “s”: “Shabbos” instead of “Shabbat”, “Toyres” instead of “Torat”. Israeli pronunciation (Sephardi in origin) gives “t” in all cases. Both pronunciations are legitimate — choose the one used in your community and stick to it.
Similar letters: how not to mix them up

items: ב (bet) and כ (kaf): bet has a small projection at the bottom right, while kaf’s bottom line curves smoothly.
ד (dalet) and ר (reish): dalet has a sharp corner with a projection, reish has a rounded one.
ה (hey), ח (chet) and ת (tav): in hey the left leg does not reach the roof; in chet it is joined to the roof; in tav the left leg is bent at the bottom.
ו (vav), ז (zayin) and ן (final nun): vav is a short stroke with a “cap” to the left, zayin has a cap on both sides, final nun reaches below the line.
ס (samech) and ם (final mem): samech is rounded at the bottom, final mem has square corners.
ע (ayin) and צ (tzadi): ayin’s tail goes down to the left, tzadi has a straight back.

blocks.text: The numerical values of the letters

The letters alef to tet stand for the units 1 to 9, yud to tzadi for the tens 10 to 90, and kuf to tav for the hundreds 100 to 400. So א = 1, י = 10, ק = 100, ת = 400. The Jewish calendar writes the year in letters: for example, תשפ״ז is the year 5787 from the creation of the world (the thousands are usually omitted). A well-known example of gematria is the word חַי (“alive”): ח = 8, י = 10, together 18. That is why in Jewish families it is customary to give gifts for celebrations in multiples of eighteen.

The order of the alphabet itself became part of the sacred texts. Many chapters of Tehillim are written as acrostics, with the lines following the letters from alef to tav: the best known is Tehillim 119, where eight verses are devoted to each letter. The hymn “Eshet Chayil” (“A Woman of Valor”, Mishlei 31:10–31), sung on Friday evening, is also arranged by the alphabet. In the daily prayers, the acrostic is Tehillim 145, “Tehillah leDavid” (Ashrei), which is recited three times a day.

How to learn: write out the letters by group and every day go over one group aloud, reading the names. Then look for familiar letters in the headings of the siddur. Usually, after two or three weeks of regular 15-minute sessions, the letters stop being “pictures”. The flashcards in this lesson will help you fix the names and sounds in your memory.

cards.front: What is the difference between פּ and פ?
cards.back: With a dagesh it is pey, “p”; without a dagesh it is fey, “f”.

cards.back: A dot over the right prong is shin, “sh”; over the left prong it is sin, “s”.

cards.back: כ→ך, מ→ם, נ→ן, פ→ף, צ→ץ (mnemonic “MaNTzePaCh”).

cards.back: “Final” — the name for the form of a letter written only at the end of a word.

cards.back: Dagesh (דָּגֵשׁ).

cards.front: What sound does the letter ח (chet) make?
cards.back: A guttural “ch”, pronounced deeper in the throat than the Russian “kh”.

cards.back: In ה the left leg does not touch the roof, in ח it does, in ת it is bent at the bottom.

cards.back: The gematria of the word חַי (“alive”): ח (8) + י (10) = 18.

cards.back: Tehillim 145, “Tehillah leDavid” (Ashrei).

cards.back: No. The only special shapes are the final forms of five letters (sofit), not capitals.

cards.back: Lamed — the only letter that rises above the line.

cards.front: How does ayin sound in modern Hebrew?
cards.back: Almost silent, like alef. In the Eastern communities ayin is a special guttural sound.

cards.back: Ktav ashuri. It is used to print the Torah, the siddur and books; the handwritten cursive looks different.

cards.back: “Eshet Chayil” (“A Woman of Valor”), Mishlei 31:10–31; it is sung on Friday evening.

cards.back: Eight verses for each letter from alef to tav — the best-known acrostic.

cards.back: It becomes a closed square; in the other four the tail goes below the line.

lessons.title: Vowel signs (nekudot) and reading syllables
citations: The Masoretic tradition (the Tiberian vocalization system)
keyIdeas: Nekudot are the signs for vowels; a Torah scroll is written without vowel signs, while the siddur and the Chumash are fully vocalized.
The vowel system was recorded in the 7th–10th centuries by the Masoretes of Tiberias, who preserved the traditional oral reading.
Kamatz and patach are “a”, tzere and segol are “e”, chirik is “i”, cholam is “o”, shuruk and kubutz are “u” (in Israeli pronunciation).

Shva na is mobile, a short “e” (at the beginning of a word and so on); shva nach is silent and closes a syllable; at the end of a word shva is not sounded, though by tradition it is written under final chaf.
Read syllable by syllable: first the letter with its vowel; the stress most often falls on the last syllable (shaLOM), and in segolate words on the second-to-last.

blocks.text: Hebrew letters represent consonants, and vowel sounds are marked with small signs — dots and dashes under a letter, above it or beside it. These signs are called **nekudot** (נְקֻדּוֹת, “dots”), and the system itself is called **nikkud**. The Torah scroll read in the synagogue has no vowel signs at all: the reader learns the text in advance from a vocalized book. But the siddur, the Chumash and children’s books are printed with full vocalization — and these are what you will learn from.

The vowel system we use today was developed by the **Masoretes** — scholars who guarded the text of the Tanakh in Tiberias (Tveria) in the 7th–10th centuries. Before that, the correct reading was passed down only orally. The Masoretes did not invent the pronunciation; they recorded the way the text had been read from generation to generation.
the system of vowel signs — marks for vowel sounds
The vowel “a”: kamatz and patach

blocks.ru: Kamatz (קָמַץ) is a small “T” shape under the letter; patach (פַּתַח) is a horizontal line. In Israeli pronunciation both give “a”.

blocks.text: In Ashkenazi pronunciation **kamatz** is read as “o”: that is why you will hear “boruch” instead of “baruch” and “Toyro” instead of “Torah”. There is also the **kamatz katan** (“small kamatz”), which sounds like “o” even in Israeli pronunciation — it appears in a closed unstressed syllable. The most common examples: כָּל — “kol” (“all, every”), חָכְמָה — “chochmah” (“wisdom”). In well-edited siddurim the kamatz katan is sometimes marked with a special shape.
The vowel “e”: tzere and segol

blocks.ru: Tzere (צֵרֵי) is two dots side by side; segol (סֶגּוֹל) is three dots in a triangle. In Israeli pronunciation both give “e”.

blocks.text: In Ashkenazi pronunciation **tzere** often sounds like “ey”: for example, “omeyn” instead of “amen”. Note: in transcription we write “e” after a consonant (be, me), although in Hebrew this vowel is firmer and closer to a clear, open “e”.
The vowel “i”: chirik

blocks.ru: Chirik (חִירִיק) is a single dot under the letter. If it is followed by the letter yud, it is “chirik male” (“full chirik”); the sound is the same.

blocks.text: The vowel “o”: cholam

blocks.ru: Cholam (חוֹלָם) is a dot above the letter, at the upper left. Cholam male is a dot over the letter vav (וֹ): here vav is not read as “v” but serves as the sign of the vowel “o”.

blocks.text: In Ashkenazi pronunciation cholam sounds like “oy” (in the Lithuanian tradition, like “ey”): “Toyro”, “sholoym”. In Israeli and Sephardi pronunciation it is a pure “o”: “Torah”, “shalom”.
The vowel “u”: shuruk and kubutz

blocks.ru: Shuruk (שׁוּרוּק) is a vav with a dot in the middle (וּ); kubutz (קֻבּוּץ) is three slanting dots under the letter. Both give “u”.

blocks.text: Be careful: וּ is not a vav with a dagesh but the vowel “u”. It is especially common at the beginning of a word as the conjunction “and” before certain letters: וּבְכָל — “u-v’chol”, “and with all”. It is easy to tell shuruk from cholam male: in shuruk the dot is **in the middle** of the vav, in cholam it is **above** it.
Shva: a short sound or a pause

blocks.ru: Shva (שְׁוָא) is two dots, one above the other, under the letter. It marks either a very short “e” or the absence of a vowel.

blocks.text: There are two kinds of shva. **Shva na** (“mobile”) is pronounced as a short “e”: at the beginning of a word (בְּרָכָה — “bracha” or “beracha”), under the second of two consecutive letters with shva, and under a letter with a strengthening dagesh. **Shva nach** (“resting”) is not pronounced at all and simply closes a syllable: יִשְׂרָאֵל — “Yis-ra-el”, where the shva under the sin is silent. At the end of a word shva is always silent, except under final chaf, where it is written by tradition: בָּרוּךְ — “baruch”.
Chatafs: shortened vowels

blocks.ru: Chataf-patach, chataf-segol and chataf-kamatz are a combination of shva with patach, segol or kamatz. They are very short “a”, “e”, “o”.

blocks.text: The guttural letters **alef, hey, chet and ayin** (א ה ח ע) do not take a simple shva and usually get a chataf instead. For example, in the word אֱלֹהֵינוּ (“our G-d”) there is a chataf-segol under the alef: “E-lo-hei-nu”. These same guttural letters, and reish, as a rule do not take a dagesh.

Another feature of the gutturals is the **patach gnuvah** (“stolen patach”): if a word ends in ח or ע with a patach, the vowel is pronounced *before* the consonant. So רוּחַ is read “ruach” (spirit), not “ruch-a”, and מַדּוּעַ is read “madua” (“why”).
Reading syllable by syllable
A syllable in Hebrew usually begins with a consonant. Read like this: first the letter, then its vowel, and only then move on to the next letter. Try reading words that appear in every prayer:

blocks.ru: “Blessed” · “are You” · “King” · “of the world (the universe)”
“Peace” · “Torah, teaching” · “commandment” · “amen” (true, so may it be)

blocks.text: In Hebrew the stress most often falls on the last syllable: shaLOM, toRAH, baRUCH, mitzVAH. But many words are stressed on the second-to-last syllable — for example, segolate words such as MElech (“king”) and Eretz (“land”), as well as some verb forms. In the Tanakh the stress is marked by the cantillation signs (te’amim), and in siddurim it is sometimes marked by a small vertical line.

Don’t be alarmed if reading is slow at first. Even experienced worshippers read an unfamiliar text syllable by syllable. A good way to practice is to read one short line from the siddur aloud every day, for example “Baruch atah Adonai Eloheinu melech ha’olam”, until it becomes familiar.
Letters that indicate vowels

In texts without vowel signs — in modern newspapers, on signs, in everyday written Hebrew — the vowels are partly hinted at by the letters **vav** and **yud**: וֹ or וּ points to “o” or “u”, י to “i” or “e”. This way of writing is called “ktiv male” (“full spelling”). So the same word can look different: in the siddur it is מִצְוָה, and in a newspaper מצווה. For prayer and Torah study, always use vocalized editions.

cards.front: What are nekudot?
cards.back: Vowel signs — marks (dots and dashes) that indicate vowel sounds.

cards.front: Does a Torah scroll have vowel signs?
cards.back: No. The reader learns the text in advance from a vocalized book.

cards.front: Who created the modern system of vowel signs?
cards.back: The Masoretes of Tiberias (7th–10th centuries), who recorded the traditional reading.

cards.front: What do kamatz and patach look like and sound like?
cards.back: Kamatz is a “T” sign under the letter, patach is a line; both are “a” (in Ashkenazi pronunciation kamatz is “o”).

cards.front: What is kamatz katan? Give an example.
cards.back: The “small kamatz”, read “o” even in Israeli pronunciation: כָּל — “kol”.

cards.front: What do tzere and segol look like?
cards.back: Tzere is two dots side by side, segol is three dots in a triangle; both are “e”.

cards.front: Which sign gives “i”?
cards.back: Chirik — a single dot under the letter (with yud it is chirik male).

cards.front: How do you tell cholam male וֹ from shuruk וּ?
cards.back: In cholam the dot is above the vav (“o”), in shuruk it is in the middle (“u”).

cards.front: What is kubutz?
cards.back: Three slanting dots under the letter; the sound is “u”, like shuruk.

cards.front: What is shva and what kinds are there?
cards.back: Two dots, one above the other. Shva na is a short “e”; shva nach is silent and closes a syllable.

cards.front: When is shva pronounced?
cards.back: At the beginning of a word, under the second of two consecutive shvas, and under a letter with a strengthening dagesh.

cards.front: What is a chataf?
cards.back: Shva combined with patach, segol or kamatz: short “a”, “e”, “o”.

cards.front: Which letters are gutturals?
cards.back: א, ה, ח, ע — they usually take a chataf instead of shva and do not take a dagesh.

cards.front: What is patach gnuvah?
cards.back: A “stolen patach” under final ח/ע: it is read before the consonant — רוּחַ “ruach”.

cards.front: Where does the stress usually fall in Hebrew?
cards.back: Most often on the last syllable (shaLOM); in segolate words, on the second-to-last (MElech).

cards.front: How is בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה read?
cards.back: “Baruch atah” — “Blessed are You”.

cards.front: What is the vowel system itself called?
cards.back: Nikkud. The individual vowel signs are called nekudot — “dots”.

cards.front: What is chirik male?
cards.back: A chirik followed by the letter yud. The sound is the same — “i” — but the spelling is full.

cards.front: How is the shuruk at the start of וּבְכָל read?
cards.back: “U-v’chol”, “and with all”: here shuruk is the vowel “u”, not the consonant “v”.

cards.front: What do the te’amim mark in the Tanakh?
cards.back: They are the cantillation signs; among other things, they mark the stress in a word.

cards.front: How is the word “mitzvah” written in a newspaper?
cards.back: מצווה — ktiv male, without vowel signs. In the siddur the same word is vocalized: מִצְוָה.

cards.front: How do Ashkenazim often read tzere?
cards.back: As “ey”: for example, “omeyn” instead of the Israeli “amen”.

cards.front: How is kamatz katan sometimes marked in a siddur?
cards.back: With a special form of the sign. It is read “o” even in Israeli pronunciation.

lessons.title: Shema Yisrael
keyIdeas: Shema Yisrael comes from Devarim 6:4; it is the declaration of G-d’s unity: “Hashem is our G-d, Hashem is One.”
In the Torah scroll the letters ע and ד are enlarged — together they spell “ed”, “witness”; the first verse is said with a drawn-out word “echad”, with the eyes covered by the right hand.
After the first verse, “Baruch shem…” is said in a whisper (these words are not in the Torah); they are said aloud only on Yom Kippur.
The Shema consists of three passages: Devarim 6:4–9, 11:13–21, and Bamidbar 15:37–41; it is read in the morning, in the evening, and before sleep.
“Ve-ahavta” speaks of love for G-d, the study of Torah, the teaching of children, tefillin and the mezuzah; the Mishnah begins with a question about the Shema.

blocks.text: “Shema Yisrael” is the central declaration of faith in Judaism. It is not a prayer of petition but a proclamation: the Almighty is the G-d of Israel, and He is One. A Jewish child learns these words among his or her very first, and they are said morning and evening, before sleep, and, by tradition, in the last minutes of life. Many people going through giyur say that the Shema became their first “own” prayer. The beit din will almost certainly ask you to recite the first line and explain its meaning.
The first verse

blocks.he: שְׁמַע יִשְׂרָאֵל ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ ה׳ אֶחָד
blocks.translit: Shema Yisrael, Adonai Eloheinu, Adonai echad
blocks.ru: Hear, O Israel: the L-rd is our G-d, the L-rd is One!

blocks.text: The verse is taken from the book of **Devarim (Deuteronomy) 6:4** — from Moshe's speech before the people entered the Land of Israel. Every word here matters. **Shema** is not just “hear” but “understand, accept, make your own.” **Yisrael** is an address to the whole people and to each of us. The four-letter Name of G-d, which in the siddur is printed in full or abbreviated (ה׳), is pronounced in prayer as **“Adonai”** (“my L-rd”), and outside prayer and study — respectfully as “HaShem” (“the Name”). **Eloheinu** means “our G-d.” **Echad** means “One”: the only one, the one and only, indivisible.

Rambam explains the word *echad* as a oneness unlike any other: G-d is not composed of parts or “persons,” and He has no body or form (Foundations of the Torah 1:7–8). Therefore, the doctrine of G-d in several persons is a false doctrine (*minut* — a denial of the Torah's principles) for Judaism, even if one tries to support it with the very words of the Shema.

In the Torah scroll, the last letter of the first word (ע in שְׁמַע) and the last letter of the last word (ד in אֶחָד) are written enlarged. Together they form the word עֵד — “witness”: by reading the Shema, a Jew bears witness to the unity of G-d. When reciting the first verse, it is customary to close one's eyes with the right hand so that nothing distracts, and to draw out the word “echad,” thinking that the Almighty rules over the whole world — the heavens, the earth, and the four directions.
“Baruch shem” — the whispered response

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ שֵׁם כְּבוֹד מַלְכוּתוֹ לְעוֹלָם וָעֶד
blocks.translit: Baruch shem kevod malchuto le'olam va'ed
blocks.ru: Blessed be the name of the glory of His kingdom forever and ever!

blocks.text: This line is not in the text of the Torah. It is an ancient response that, according to tradition, was recited in the Temple when the high priest pronounced the Name of G-d. The Talmud (Pesachim 56a) relates that the patriarch Yaakov gathered his sons before his death, and they said to him, “Shema Yisrael” — “Hear, O Israel (that is, Yaakov), the L-rd is One,” and he answered, “Baruch shem…”. Since these words are not from the Torah, they are said **in a whisper** — all year except Yom Kippur, when they are said aloud.
The first paragraph: “Ve-ahavta”

After the first verse comes a passage known by its first word — **“Ve-ahavta”** (“And you shall love”). These are the verses of Devarim 6:5–9. They speak of love for G-d, of the study of Torah, of raising children, and of tefillin and the mezuzah.

blocks.he: וְאָהַבְתָּ אֵת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ בְּכָל־לְבָבְךָ וּבְכָל־נַפְשְׁךָ וּבְכָל־מְאֹדֶךָ׃
blocks.translit: Ve'ahavta et Adonai Elohecha bechol levavcha uvechol nafshecha uvechol me'odecha.
blocks.ru: And you shall love the L-rd your G-d with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your might.

blocks.he: וְהָיוּ הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי מְצַוְּךָ הַיּוֹם עַל־לְבָבֶךָ׃
blocks.translit: Vehayu hadvarim ha'eleh asher anochi metzavcha hayom al levavecha.
blocks.ru: And these words, which I command you this day, shall be upon your heart.

blocks.he: וְשִׁנַּנְתָּם לְבָנֶיךָ וְדִבַּרְתָּ בָּם בְּשִׁבְתְּךָ בְּבֵיתֶךָ וּבְלֶכְתְּךָ בַדֶּרֶךְ וּבְשָׁכְבְּךָ וּבְקוּמֶךָ׃
blocks.translit: Veshinantam levanacha vedibarta bam beshivtecha beveitecha uvelechtecha vaderach uvshochbecha uvkumecha.
blocks.ru: And you shall teach them diligently to your children, and speak of them when you sit in your house, and when you walk on the way, and when you lie down, and when you rise up.

blocks.he: וּקְשַׁרְתָּם לְאוֹת עַל־יָדֶךָ וְהָיוּ לְטֹטָפֹת בֵּין עֵינֶיךָ׃
blocks.translit: Ukshartam le'ot al yadecha vehayu letotafot bein einecha.
blocks.ru: And you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as frontlets (totafot) between your eyes.
And you shall write them upon the doorposts of your house and on your gates.

blocks.text: The Sages interpret the three measures of love as follows: “with all your heart” — with both of your inclinations, the good and the evil, that is, with your entire nature; “with all your soul” — even if you must give your life; “with all your might” — with all your possessions and all your strength (Mishnah Berachot 9:5). From verse 7 is derived the mitzvah of teaching Torah and passing it on to one's children, as well as the very obligation to read the Shema — “when you lie down and when you rise up,” that is, in the evening and in the morning. Verse 8 is the source of the mitzvah of tefillin, verse 9 of the mezuzah. Thus a whole program of Jewish life is contained in six verses.
The three passages of the Shema

items: **Devarim 6:4–9** — the “Shema” and “Ve-ahavta”: accepting upon oneself “the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven,” the unity of G-d, and love for Him.
**Devarim 11:13–21** — “Ve'haya im shamoa”: reward and responsibility, accepting “the yoke of the mitzvot”; tefillin, the mezuzah, and the study of Torah are repeated.
**Bamidbar (Numbers) 15:37–41** — “Va'yomer”: the mitzvah of tzitzit and the remembrance of the Exodus from Egypt.

blocks.text: The Mishnah (Berachot 2:2) explains this order: first a person accepts upon himself the sovereignty of Heaven, and then the mitzvot. The full reading of the Shema includes all three passages and the blessings surrounding them: in the morning, two before the Shema and one after; in the evening, two before and two after.
When the Shema is read

items: **In the morning** — in the Shacharit prayer.
**In the evening** — in the Maariv prayer, after the stars come out.
**Before sleep** — the “Shema al ha-mita,” at least the first passage, together with the blessing “ha-Mapil.”
At the end of the Neilah prayer on Yom Kippur, the first verse is recited by the entire congregation.
By tradition, these are a Jew's last words before death — thus died Rabbi Akiva (Berachot 61b).

blocks.text: The Mishnah begins precisely with a question about the Shema: “From what time may the Shema be read in the evening?” (Berachot 1:1). The Sages placed this question at the very beginning of the Oral Torah — so important is this mitzvah.

By halacha, men are obligated to read the Shema in the morning and in the evening. The morning Shema must be read by the end of the **third “hour” of the day** (here an hour is one twelfth of the daylight hours, the so-called “sha'ah zmanit”); the evening Shema — after the stars come out, preferably before midnight, and at the latest before dawn. The first verse is recited with special concentration (kavanah): if a person recited it without thinking of its meaning, he has not fulfilled the mitzvah. The words must be pronounced clearly, without running the end of one word into the beginning of the next. Women are exempt from the Shema by halacha, as it is a time-bound mitzvah, but it is customary for them to recite at least the first verse.

If you do not yet read Hebrew fluently — that is all right. The Mishnah permits reading the Shema in any language a person understands (Sotah 7:1). But it is worth trying to learn at least the first two lines in Hebrew: millions of Jews around the world say them together.

The first verse of the Shema, “Baruch shem,” and “Ve-ahavta” are found in the siddurim of all streams of Judaism — they are the common heritage of the entire people. Learn them by heart: you will be able to recite them in any synagogue in the world.

differs.text: Reform Judaism does not regard the time of reading the Shema as a strict halachic obligation. The second passage (Devarim 11:13–21), with its idea of direct reward through rain and harvest, was traditionally omitted or replaced in Reform siddurim; in “Mishkan T'filah” it is given as an option.

blocks.text: Every day the Shema returns you to a simple assertion: the L-rd is One. The unity spoken of by the word *echad* is not composed of parts and “persons,” and in prayer we turn to Him alone. If you later hear that the very text of the Shema allows a “composite” G-d, return to these words and to how Rambam reads *echad*.

lessons.title: The Amidah and the three daily prayers
keyIdeas: The Amidah (“standing”; it is also called the Shmoneh Esreh) is the main prayer, recited standing; on weekdays it has 19 blessings.
The structure of the Amidah: praise (1–3), petitions (4–16), thanksgiving (17–19) — like a subject standing before a king.
The three daily prayers are Shacharit, Mincha, and Maariv; on Shabbat, festivals, and Rosh Chodesh Musaf is added, and on Yom Kippur — Neilah.

The Talmud gives two explanations: the prayers were instituted by the patriarchs, and the prayers themselves correspond to the sacrifices in the Temple; after the destruction of the Temple, prayer replaced the sacrifices.

The Amidah is prayed quietly, following the example of Chana, facing Jerusalem; before beginning — three steps back and three forward, at the end — three steps back; in the 13th blessing we also pray for the righteous gerim.

blocks.text: If the Shema is the declaration of faith, then the **Amidah** is the heart of prayer. The word “amidah” means “standing”: this prayer is recited standing, with concentration, as if a person were standing before the King. It is also called the **“Shmoneh Esreh”** — “Eighteen,” after the original number of blessings, and in the Talmud simply “ha-Tefillah,” “the Prayer.” When the Sages speak of “prayer” without qualification, they mean the Amidah.
“Standing”; the main prayer of every service, recited standing
The three daily prayers

items: **Shacharit** (שַׁחֲרִית) — the morning prayer, from dawn; it includes the morning blessings, psalms, the Shema with its blessings, and the Amidah.
**Mincha** (מִנְחָה) — the daytime prayer, from afternoon until sunset; the shortest one: Ashrei, the Amidah, and the concluding prayers.
**Maariv** (מַעֲרִיב), or Arvit — the evening prayer, after nightfall; it includes the Shema with its blessings and the Amidah.

blocks.text: Already in the Tanakh there is mention of praying three times a day: King David writes, “Evening, and morning, and at noon I pray” (Tehillim 55:18), and the prophet Daniel in Babylon “knelt upon his knees three times a day and prayed” by windows open toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:11). The Talmud (Berachot 26b) gives two explanations: the prayers were instituted by the patriarchs — Avraham the morning prayer, Yitzchak the afternoon prayer, Yaakov the evening prayer; and the prayers correspond to the daily sacrifices in the Temple. After the destruction of the Temple, prayer became the “service of the heart” — it replaced the sacrifices.

On Shabbat, festivals, and Rosh Chodesh, **Musaf** (the “additional” prayer) is added, corresponding to the additional sacrifice in the Temple. On Yom Kippur there is a fifth prayer — **Neilah**, the “closing of the gates.”
Structure: praise, petitions, thanksgiving

According to the Talmud (Megillah 17b), the text of the Amidah was arranged by the “Men of the Great Assembly” at the beginning of the era of the Second Temple. Later, in the time of Rabban Gamliel in Yavneh, one more blessing was added — against informers and apostates (Berachot 28b) — so that today the weekday Amidah has **19 blessings**, although the name “Eighteen” has remained. They are all divided into three parts — just as a subject addresses a king: first he praises, then he petitions, then he gives thanks.

items: **Praise (1–3):** 1) Avot — the G-d of the patriarchs Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov; 2) Gevurot — the might of G-d, who gives life and sends rain; 3) Kedushat ha-Shem — the holiness of G-d.

**Petitions (4–16):** 4) understanding and knowledge; 5) return (teshuvah); 6) forgiveness; 7) redemption; 8) healing; 9) blessing of the harvest and the year; 10) the ingathering of the exiles; 11) the restoration of righteous judgment; 12) against informers and evildoers; 13) for the righteous and the gerim — the righteous converts; 14) the rebuilding of Jerusalem; 15) the revival of the kingdom of the house of David; 16) “Who hears prayer.”

**Thanksgiving (17–19):** 17) Avodah — for the acceptance of our service and for the return of the Shechinah to Zion; 18) Modim — thanksgiving “for Your wonders that are with us every day”; 19) Shalom — a plea for peace.

blocks.text: Three blessings of the Amidah — for the ingathering of the exiles (the 10th), for Jerusalem and “the throne of David” (the 14th), and “Et Tzemach David” (the 15th) — ask for what still lies ahead: “for Your salvation we hope all day.” Every day a Jew prays for the coming of Mashiach, because he has not yet come (Rambam, Laws of Kings 11:1, 11:4). In prayer one turns only to the Almighty, directly and without an intermediary — not to an angel, not to a human being, not to any image (Rambam, 5th Principle); one who places an intermediary between himself and G-d, Rambam classifies among the *minim* (Laws of Repentance 3:7).

Note the 13th blessing: it contains the words “and for the righteous gerim” (וְעַל גֵּרֵי הַצֶּדֶק). Every day, three times a day, the entire Jewish people prays for those who joined it through giyur. After your giyur, you will be praying — among others — for yourself.

On Shabbat and festivals the middle petitions are not said — on this day it is not fitting to ask for everyday needs. Therefore the Shabbat Amidah has **seven blessings**: the first three, the last three, and one middle blessing devoted to the holiness of the day.
How the Amidah begins

blocks.he: אֲדֹנָי שְׂפָתַי תִּפְתָּח וּפִי יַגִּיד תְּהִלָּתֶךָ
blocks.translit: Adonai, sefatai tiftach ufi yagid tehilatecha
blocks.ru: L-rd, open my lips, and my mouth shall declare Your praise.

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ וֵאלֹהֵי אֲבוֹתֵינוּ, אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם, אֱלֹהֵי יִצְחָק, וֵאלֹהֵי יַעֲקֹב
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu ve'Elohei avoteinu, Elohei Avraham, Elohei Yitzchak ve'Elohei Yaakov
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd, our G-d and the G-d of our fathers, the G-d of Avraham, the G-d of Yitzchak, and the G-d of Yaakov.

blocks.text: How the Amidah is prayed

The Sages took Chana, the mother of the prophet Shmuel, as the model for prayer: “Chana spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard” (Shmuel I 1:13). From this comes the rule: the Amidah is recited **quietly**, moving the lips so that only the one praying can hear. One prays standing, facing Jerusalem (in Jerusalem — toward the Temple Mount). Before beginning, one takes three steps back and three steps forward — as if approaching the King — and at the end three steps back, as if taking leave.

Halachic details: the feet are placed together, after the model of the angels, of whom it is said “their feet were a straight foot” (Yechezkel 1:7). One bows four times — at the beginning and end of the first blessing and at the beginning and end of the blessing of Modim: at the word “baruch” one bends the knees, at “atah” one bows, and at the pronunciation of the Name one straightens up. During the Amidah one may not interrupt, respond to a greeting, or walk directly in front of someone praying. It is best to recite the morning Amidah by the end of the fourth hour of the day, though in an extreme case one may do so until noon (Mishnah Berachot 4:1).
The minyan and the cantor's repetition

Some parts of the prayer are recited only in a **minyan** — a gathering of ten adult Jews. The Talmud (Megillah 23b) teaches: “every matter of holiness — no fewer than ten.” These are Kaddish, Kedushah (the insert “Holy, holy, holy”), “Barchu,” the public reading of the Torah, and **the cantor's repetition of the Amidah** (chazarat hashatz): after the silent prayer, the leader (shaliach tzibbur) recites the Amidah aloud, and the congregation answers “amen.” The Sages derive the number ten from the word “congregation” (eidah), by which the Torah called the ten spies (Bamidbar 14:27). One may pray alone too — prayer is accepted everywhere — but prayer with the congregation is especially valued.
In Orthodox Judaism, only men over the age of 13 (after bar mitzvah) are counted in the minyan.

differs.text: In most Masorti (Conservative) congregations, women have been counted in the minyan on equal terms with men since 1973; there are also non-egalitarian Conservative congregations.
In Reform Judaism men and women are fully equal in prayer; many congregations do not require a minyan for Kaddish and other parts of the service.

blocks.text: Be careful in the reading of the Shema and in prayer. And when you pray, do not make your prayer a fixed routine, but a plea for mercy before the All-Present.

This thought of Rabbi Shimon is the key to prayer. The text of the Amidah is fixed, but the Sages permitted adding one's own requests in one's own words in the blessing “Who hears prayer,” and at the end of the Amidah, before the final steps — a personal prayer in any language.

In Reform and Conservative siddurim the text of the Amidah is partly changed. Masorti (“Siddur Sim Shalom”) largely keeps the traditional text, but speaks of the Temple sacrifices in the past tense and, at one's option, adds the matriarchs to the first blessing — Sarah, Rivka, Rachel, and Leah.

differs.text: The Reform siddur “Mishkan T'filah” adds the matriarchs, offers in the second blessing “mechaye hakol” (“who gives life to all”) alongside “mechaye hametim” (“who gives life to the dead”), replaces the curse against informers with a general prayer for the uprooting of evil, and does not ask for the restoration of the sacrifices. The fixed times of prayer are regarded as a valuable tradition rather than an obligation.

blocks.text: The Amidah is recited standing, facing Jerusalem, and one turns only to the Almighty. The blessings for the ingathering of the exiles and for Jerusalem are petitions for what still lies ahead, and they are said directly to Him, without an intermediary and without turning to a human being, an angel, or an image (Rambam, 5th Principle).

cards.front: Which direction do we face in prayer?
cards.back: Facing Jerusalem.

cards.front: What is a minyan?
cards.back: A gathering of ten adult Jews, required for Kaddish, Kedushah and the Torah reading.

cards.front: Who counts toward a minyan according to Orthodox halacha?
cards.back: Ten men older than 13.

differs.text: In most Masorti communities, women too, on equal footing with men.
Men and women on equal footing; a minyan is often not required.

cards.front: What is Musaf?
cards.back: The additional prayer on Shabbat, festivals and Rosh Chodesh.

cards.front: How many times do we bow in the Amidah?
cards.back: Four: at the beginning and end of the first blessing and of Modim.

cards.front: What does the Talmud call the Amidah for short?
cards.back: "Ha-Tefillah" ("the Prayer"): when the Sages say "prayer" without further specification, they mean the Amidah.

cards.front: What else is Maariv called?
cards.back: Arvit. It is the evening prayer after nightfall.

cards.front: What is Neilah?
cards.back: The fifth prayer of Yom Kippur. The name means "the closing of the gates."

cards.front: Where in the Tanakh is the thrice-daily prayer mentioned?
cards.back: Tehillim 55:18: David prays "evening, and morning, and at noon."

cards.front: Where were the windows by which Daniel prayed facing?
cards.back: Toward Jerusalem; he prayed three times a day (Daniel 6:11).

cards.front: Where in the Amidah can one add one's own words?
cards.back: In the blessing "Who hears prayer" and at the end, before the final steps, in any language.

cards.front: What does Rabbi Shimon teach in Pirkei Avot 2:13?
cards.back: Not to make prayer a fixed, rote duty, but a plea for mercy before the Omnipresent One.

cards.front: To Whom is the Amidah addressed?
cards.back: Only to the Almighty, directly, without an intermediary — not to an angel, a human being, or an image (Rambam, 5th principle; Laws of Repentance 3:7).

cards.front: Why is "Et Tzemach David" requested every day in the Amidah?
cards.back: The Mashiach from the house of David has not yet come; we await him: "for Your salvation we hope all day" (the 15th blessing).

lessons.title: Blessings (berachot)
keyIdeas: Berachot are said for pleasures, for mitzvot and as praises; Rabbi Meir taught to recite a hundred blessings a day.
Every berachah begins: "Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam"; for mitzvot one continues "asher kidshanu be-mitzvotav ve-tzivanu".

For bread — "ha-motzi lechem min ha'aretz", for wine — "borei pri ha-gafen", for fruit of the tree — "borei pri ha-etz", for fruit of the ground — "borei pri ha-adamah", for what does not grow from the ground — "she-hakol".
Birkat HaMazon after a meal with bread is a mitzvah of the Torah (Devarim 8:10); "Modeh Ani" is said immediately upon waking.
"Shehecheyanu" is said over something new and joyful; a mezuzah is a parchment with the first passages of the Shema on the doorpost.

blocks.text: Jewish life is literally permeated with blessings. Before eating and after, upon waking in the morning, before performing a mitzvah, at the sight of a rainbow or at a new joyful milestone — there is a **berachah** (בְּרָכָה, pl. **berachot**) for everything. Rabbi Meir taught that a person must recite a hundred blessings every day (Menachot 43b), and in the ordinary routine of prayers and meals one indeed reaches about a hundred. A berachah turns an everyday action into a moment of meeting with the Almighty.

Why bless? The Talmud (Berachot 35a) explains: "The earth is the L-rd's, and all that fills it" (Tehillim 24:1), and one who enjoys the world without a blessing is like one who takes what is not his. A blessing is the recognition that everything is given to us as a gift. Therefore berachot fall into three main types:

items: **Blessings over pleasures** (birkot ha-nehenin) — before eating, drinking, or enjoying a pleasant fragrance.
**Blessings over mitzvot** (birkot ha-mitzvot) — before performing a mitzvah: lighting candles, putting on tefillin, affixing a mezuzah.
**Blessings of praise and thanksgiving** — at the sight of wonders of nature, at joyful and even sad events.

blocks.text: The formula of a blessing

blocks.he: בָּרוּךְ אַתָּה ה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ מֶלֶךְ הָעוֹלָם
blocks.translit: Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam
blocks.ru: Blessed are You, L-rd our G-d, King of the universe…

blocks.text: The striking thing in this formula is the transition: it begins with a direct address — "You" — and continues in the third person — "King of the universe," "who sanctified us." The commentators see in this two aspects of our relationship with G-d: He is near, He can be addressed as "you," — and at the same time He is the incomprehensible Master of the world. The words "King of the universe" (melech ha-olam) are indispensable: a blessing without mention of the Name and the Kingship is not considered complete.

blocks.ru: …who sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us…

blocks.text: This is how all blessings over mitzvot begin. After the words "and commanded us," the specific mitzvah is named. For example, before a meal with bread, the hands are washed from a vessel and one says "…al netilat yadayim" ("…concerning the washing of the hands").
Blessings before food

blocks.ru: …who brings forth bread from the earth.
…who creates the fruit of the vine (for wine and grape juice).
…who creates the fruit of the tree (for fruits from trees).
…who creates the fruit of the ground (for vegetables, bananas, potatoes, etc.).
…who creates the various kinds of food (for baked goods and dishes of the five grains, other than bread).
…through Whose word everything comes into being (for water, meat, fish, milk, eggs, drinks, etc.).

blocks.text: The Mishnah (Berachot 6:1) establishes the principle: for the fruit of a tree one says "borei pri ha-etz," except for wine, over which one says "borei pri ha-gafen"; for fruit of the ground — "borei pri ha-adamah," except for bread, over which one says "ha-motzi." Bread and wine are the most important foods, and they have their own special blessings. The blessing over bread "covers" the whole meal: if you started with bread, the remaining dishes are usually not blessed separately. For what does not grow from the ground — "she-hakol" (Berachot 6:3). Sephardim pronounce "ha-gefen" and "nihye"; this is a difference of pronunciation, not of meaning.

The details of determining the correct blessing (for example, for mixed dishes, juices, rice) and the order of priority when several kinds of food are before you are treated in the halachic literature. If you are in doubt which blessing to say, "she-hakol" after the fact (bedi'avad) counts for any food, but one should not do so in advance.
Birkat HaMazon — thanksgiving after a meal

blocks.he: וְאָכַלְתָּ וְשָׂבָעְתָּ וּבֵרַכְתָּ אֶת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ עַל הָאָרֶץ הַטֹּבָה אֲשֶׁר נָתַן לָךְ
blocks.translit: Ve-achalta ve-savata u-verachta et Adonai Elohecha al ha'aretz ha-tovah asher natan lakh
blocks.ru: And you shall eat, and be satisfied, and bless the L-rd your G-d for the good land that He has given you.

blocks.text: Blessings before a meal were instituted by the Sages, while thanksgiving **after** a meal with bread is a mitzvah of the Torah itself (Devarim 8:10). This is **Birkat HaMazon** ("blessing for the food"), popularly called "bentsching" in Yiddish. It consists of four blessings: for food for the whole world (according to tradition, composed by Moshe), for the Land of Israel (Yehoshua), for the rebuilding of Jerusalem (David and Shlomo), and "Ha-tov ve-ha-meitiv" ("the Good and the Doer of good"), added by the Sages in Yavneh (Berachot 48b). If three or more adults are at the table, a **zimun** — a joint invitation to bless — is made before Birkat HaMazon. After other foods, short concluding blessings are said: "Borei Nefashot" or "Al HaMichyah."
"Modeh Ani" — the first words of the day

blocks.he: מוֹדֶה אֲנִי לְפָנֶיךָ מֶלֶךְ חַי וְקַיָּם, שֶׁהֶחֱזַרְתָּ בִּי נִשְׁמָתִי בְּחֶמְלָה, רַבָּה אֱמוּנָתֶךָ
blocks.translit: Modeh ani lefanecha, melech chai ve-kayam, she-hechezarta bi nishmati be-chemlah, rabbah emunatecha
blocks.ru: I give thanks before You, living and everlasting King, for You have returned my soul to me in Your mercy; great is Your faithfulness.

blocks.text: These words are said immediately upon waking, still in bed. In tradition, sleep is compared to a small death, and waking to the return of the soul. "Modeh Ani" does not contain G-d's Name, so it may be said before washing the hands. A woman says "**Modah Ani**" (מוֹדָה). Pay attention to the ending: "great is Your faithfulness" — G-d returns our soul to us, entrusting us with a new day.
"Shehecheyanu" — for what is new and joyful

blocks.ru: …who has granted us life, sustained us, and enabled us to reach this time.

blocks.text: This is a blessing of joy. The Mishnah (Berachot 9:3) prescribes saying it for one who has built a new house or bought new things. By custom, "Shehecheyanu" is said at the beginning of festivals (at kiddush and the lighting of candles), on the first evening of Chanukah, over the first fruit of the season, and when buying important new clothing. Many say it on the day of their giyur — for example, after immersion in the mikveh — although customs vary from community to community here.
Mezuzah

The mitzvah of the mezuzah is taken from the Shema: "And you shall write them on the doorposts of your house and on your gates" (Devarim 6:9; 11:20). A mezuzah is a parchment (klaf) on which a sofer (scribe) writes by hand the first two passages of the Shema: Devarim 6:4–9 and 11:13–21. The scroll is rolled up, placed in a case, and affixed to the right-hand doorpost (as one enters). Passing by, many people touch the mezuzah with their hand and kiss their fingers — as a sign of love for the mitzvot.

blocks.ru: …who sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us to affix a mezuzah.

blocks.text: By halacha, the mezuzah is affixed on the upper third of the doorpost — Ashkenazim place it slantwise, with the upper end pointing into the room; Sephardim place it vertically. A mezuzah is needed on every doorway of living rooms, but not in the bathroom or toilet. Outside Israel, in rented housing, the mezuzah may be affixed within 30 days of moving in (Menachot 44a). A mezuzah at home is checked by a sofer twice in seven years (Yoma 11a), since the letters may be damaged. A purchased "mezuzah" without a kosher handwritten parchment inside is just a case.

The mezuzah, "Modeh Ani," "ha-motzi" and "Shehecheyanu" are practical things a beit din often asks about: "Which blessing would you say over an apple? And over bread? What do you say in the morning?" Try blessing every meal for a week — it is the best way to memorize them.

differs.text: In Reform communities berachot are recited according to the same formulas, but their observance is a matter of personal choice rather than a halachic obligation; many siddurim offer an abbreviated Birkat HaMazon and gender-inclusive forms of address.

lessons.title: Siddur, synagogue, tallit, tefillin and kippah
keyIdeas: The siddur is the prayer book for weekdays and Shabbat, the machzor for Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and festivals; there are different nusachim.
The synagogue (beit knesset) is a "small Sanctuary": an aron kodesh for Torah scrolls, a bimah, a ner tamid; on entering, many say "Ma Tovu."
Tzitzit are fringes on the four corners of a garment, reminding of the mitzvot; the tallit gadol is put on for the morning prayer.
Tefillin are two boxes with four passages of the Torah: on the biceps of the weaker arm, opposite the heart, and on the head; they are worn on weekdays, but not on Shabbat or festivals.
The kippah is an ancient custom of awe before Heaven ("the Shechinah is above me"), not a mitzvah of the Torah; in the synagogue the head is covered in all streams of Judaism.

blocks.text: The siddur and the machzor

The **siddur** (סִדּוּר, "order") is the prayer book for weekdays and Shabbat. The first known complete siddur was compiled by Rav Amram Gaon in Babylonia in the 9th century; in the 10th century Rav Saadia Gaon created his own siddur with explanations in Arabic. For Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur and the pilgrimage festivals there is a special prayer book — the **machzor** ("cycle").

In different communities their own **nusachim** developed — variants of the text and order of prayers: Nusach Ashkenaz (Eastern and Western Europe), Nusach Sefard (adopted by the Hasidim and based on the teachings of the Kabbalists), Nusach Ari (Chabad) and Nusach Edot HaMizrach (Sephardi and Eastern communities). The differences concern individual words, the order of psalms and customs, but the foundation — the Shema, the Amidah, the blessings — is the same everywhere. In Russian, the siddurim "Vrata Molitvy" ("Gates of Prayer") and editions with a parallel translation are widespread. The movements have their own siddurim: in the Masorti movement — "Sim Shalom" and "Lev Shalem," among Reform Jews — "Mishkan T'filah." Choose the siddur accepted in your community.

Reform communities pray from their own siddurim in which the classical framework (the Shema, the Amidah, the blessings) is preserved, but the text is often given in Hebrew and in the community's language side by side, and some formulations are reworked. In North America the main siddur today is **Mishkan T'filah** (CCAR Press, 2007), which replaced **Gates of Prayer** (1975). For the Days of Awe a machzor, **Mishkan HaNefesh**, has been published. In these books the matriarchs (Sarah, Rivka, Rachel and Leah) are often included in the Amidah alongside the patriarchs; some blessings offer variants — for example, "mechayeh ha-kol" ("who gives life to all") alongside the traditional "mechayeh ha-meitim" ("who revives the dead"). The exact formulations depend on the edition and the community.

Prayer in a language one understands is, in Reform Judaism, not a concession and not a replacement of "real" Hebrew, but a conscious principle: a person must understand what he says to the Almighty. Hebrew remains the sacred language of the people, and communities study it, read the Torah and sing the main blessings in Hebrew. In many progressive synagogues instrumental music is heard on Shabbat, men and women lead the service on equal footing, and there are women rabbis and rabbis from among the gerim. In the Russian-speaking communities of ROOPI the siddur may differ in composition from the North American Mishkan T'filah: rely on the book of your synagogue and compare it with what is given in this app (Nusach Ashkenaz).
Synagogue

In Hebrew, the synagogue is the **beit knesset** ("house of assembly"). It does not replace the Temple, but the Sages call it a "small Sanctuary" (mikdash me'at). In a synagogue there is the **aron kodesh** — a cabinet for Torah scrolls on the wall facing Jerusalem; the **bimah** — the platform from which the Torah is read; and the **ner tamid** — the ever-burning lamp in memory of the Temple menorah. On entering, many recite the verse:

blocks.he: מַה טֹּבוּ אֹהָלֶיךָ יַעֲקֹב מִשְׁכְּנֹתֶיךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל
blocks.translit: Ma tovu ohalecha Yaakov, mishkenotecha Yisrael
blocks.ru: How beautiful are your tents, Yaakov, your dwellings, Israel!

blocks.text: In an Orthodox synagogue men and women pray separately: a **mechitzah** (partition) separates them, or the women sit in a separate gallery — the **ezrat nashim**. This is done so that nothing distracts from prayer.

differs.text: In most Masorti synagogues men and women sit together; there are also communities with separate seating.
In Reform synagogues mixed seating has been customary since the 19th century; men and women take part in the service on equal footing.

blocks.text: A kippah, a tallit, a menorah and a Jewish name do not yet make a congregation your people's synagogue. Before joining a new community, it is worth finding out whether one of the known movements of Judaism recognizes it and what they believe there about G-d, about the Mashiach and about the Torah. If in doubt, ask your rabbi. It is better to ask a calm question in advance than to untangle a muddle later.
Tallit and tzitzit

blocks.he: וְעָשׂוּ לָהֶם צִיצִת עַל כַּנְפֵי בִגְדֵיהֶם לְדֹרֹתָם
blocks.translit: Ve-asu lahem tzitzit al kanfei vigdeihem le-dorotam
blocks.ru: And they shall make themselves fringes on the corners of their garments throughout their generations.

blocks.text: **Tzitzit** are fringes on the four corners of a garment. The Torah explains their meaning: "and you shall look upon them and remember all the mitzvot of the L-rd, and do them" (Bamidbar 15:39). The **tallit** (tallit gadol) is the large woolen shawl with tzitzit that is worn during the morning prayer; the **tallit katan** is a small four-cornered garment with tzitzit worn all day under the shirt. Before wrapping oneself in the tallit, one says the blessing:

blocks.ru: …who sanctified us with His mitzvot and commanded us to wrap ourselves in the tzitzit.

blocks.text: Halachic details: four threads are threaded into each of the four fringes and folded double — making eight ends; five double knots are tied, between which Ashkenazim make 7, 8, 11 and 13 windings. The tallit is worn by day, at Shacharit (and on Yom Kippur also in the evening). Among many Ashkenazim (of Polish and Lithuanian origin) a man begins to wear the large tallit only after his wedding, while among Sephardim and German Jews — from the bar mitzvah. Over the tallit katan one says the blessing "al mitzvat tzitzit" (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 9).
Tefillin

**Tefillin** are two black leather boxes with straps. Inside are parchments with four passages of the Torah where this mitzvah is spoken of: Shemot 13:1–10, Shemot 13:11–16, Devarim 6:4–9 and Devarim 11:13–21. The mitzvah follows directly from the Shema: "and you shall bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes" (Devarim 6:8). The **tefillin shel yad** is put on the biceps of the weaker arm (the left one for a right-hander), opposite the heart; the **tefillin shel rosh** — on the head above the hairline. In this way a person dedicates to G-d both feelings and thoughts and actions. Tefillin are put on on weekdays during the morning prayer; on Shabbat and festivals they are not put on, because these days themselves are a "sign" between G-d and Israel.

blocks.ru: …who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to put on tefillin.

blocks.text: Halachic details: the obligation begins at bar mitzvah (age 13). First the hand tefillin is put on and tied, then the head tefillin; they are removed in the reverse order. Ashkenazim say two blessings — “l'haniach tefillin” over the hand tefillin and “al mitzvat tefillin” over the head tefillin; Sephardim say one, over the hand tefillin. The strap of the hand tefillin is wound around the forearm seven times (Ashkenazim wind it away from themselves, Sephardim and Chassidim toward themselves). The parchments are written by a sofer; tefillin must be checked and kosher (Kitzur Shulchan Aruch 10).
Kippah

The **kippah** (in Yiddish, yarmulke) is a small cap that covers the head. It is not a commandment of the Torah but an ancient custom expressing awe before Heaven: the Talmud tells of a sage who would not walk even four cubits with his head uncovered, saying: “The Shechinah is above me” (Kiddushin 31a). Over time the custom became universally accepted: in Orthodox circles men always cover their heads, and in the synagogue heads are covered in all movements. The color and material of a kippah often indicate belonging to one community or another, but they have no halachic significance.
Women and Prayer

The Mishnah (Berachot 3:3) teaches that women are exempt from the Shema and tefillin but **are obligated in prayer**, mezuzah and Birkat HaMazon. The general principle: women are exempt from positive commandments bound to a specific time (Mishnah Kiddushin 1:7) — for example, tzitzit and tefillin. Prayer, however, is a plea for mercy, and everyone is obligated in it.

In Orthodox Judaism women are not counted in a minyan, do not lead public prayer, and usually do not put on tefillin or a tallit. Many women pray Shacharit and Minchah every day, or at least say a short personal prayer with blessings; in some Modern Orthodox communities there are women's prayer groups.

differs.text: Most Masorti communities are egalitarian: since 1973 women have been counted in a minyan, and since 1985 women have been ordained as rabbis (Jewish Theological Seminary, New York). Women may lead prayer, read the Torah, and put on a tallit and tefillin; the Masorti Committee on Jewish Law recognizes that they bear an equal obligation in these mitzvot. Some communities remain non-egalitarian.

Reform Judaism is fully egalitarian: women serve as rabbis (the first in the USA was Sally Priesand, 1972; even earlier, in 1935 in Germany, Regina Jonas), cantors and service leaders. Tallit, kippah and tefillin are a personal choice for men and women alike.

blocks.text: Before the beit din, be ready to describe how your community prays: where men and women sit, when the tallit and tefillin are put on, which siddur is used. If you are a man undergoing an Orthodox or Conservative giyur, learn to put on tefillin ahead of time — ask someone in the community to show you.

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of the Amidah. Why is it built this way?
questions.modelAnswer: The Amidah is the central prayer of every service; it is said standing, quietly, facing Jerusalem. On weekdays it has 19 blessings: the first three are praise (Avot, Gevurot, Kedushat HaShem), the middle thirteen are requests (wisdom, teshuvah, forgiveness, healing, harvest, Jerusalem and others), and the last three are thanksgiving (Avodah, Modim, Shalom). This is how a subject comes before a king: first he praises, then he asks, then he gives thanks and departs. On Shabbat the requests are replaced by a single blessing on the holiness of the day — making seven. The sages permitted adding personal requests in one's own words.

questions.prompt: Why does a Jew pray three times a day, and what did prayer replace after the destruction of the Temple?
questions.modelAnswer: Already in the Tanakh David speaks of prayer “evening, morning and noon” (Tehillim 55:18), and Daniel prayed three times a day, facing Jerusalem (Daniel 6:11). The Talmud (Berachot 26b) gives two explanations: the prayers were instituted by the Patriarchs, and the prayers correspond to the daily Temple offerings. After the destruction of the Temple, the “service of the heart” — prayer — took the place of the offerings. Therefore Shacharit and Minchah correspond to the morning and afternoon offerings, and on festivals Musaf is added.

differs.text: Reform Judaism sees the three prayers as a valuable tradition rather than an obligation, and does not pray for the restoration of the sacrificial offerings.

A bracha is not information for G-d but a change in me: it teaches me to see food as a gift rather than something to take for granted. The formula “Baruch atah Adonai, Eloheinu melech ha'olam” reminds us that G-d is both close (“You”) and the Master of the universe. Blessings turn ordinary actions into service; Rabbi Meir advised saying a hundred blessings a day.

questions.modelAnswer: According to the Mishnah (Berachot 3:3), women are obligated to pray but are exempt from time-bound commandments (Kiddushin 1:7) such as tefillin and tzitzit. In an Orthodox synagogue men and women sit separately, behind a mechitzah; only men are counted in a minyan, and men lead the prayers. I pray as is customary in my community and respect the practice of others.

questions.prompt: What are tefillin and where does this mitzvah come from? (For a male candidate: do you know how to put them on?)
questions.modelAnswer: Tefillin are two leather boxes containing parchments on which four passages of the Torah are written: Shemot 13:1–10, 13:11–16, Devarim 6:4–9 and 11:13–21. The mitzvah comes from the Shema: “Bind them as a sign upon your hand, and they shall be as frontlets between your eyes” (Devarim 6:8). The hand tefillin is placed on the biceps of the weaker arm, opposite the heart, and the head tefillin above the hairline; in this way a person dedicates their heart, thoughts and deeds to G-d. Tefillin are worn on weekdays during Shacharit, but not on Shabbat and festivals. First the hand tefillin is put on with the blessing “lehaniach tefillin”, and then the head tefillin.

questions.prompt: Why pray in Hebrew if the Almighty understands every language?
questions.modelAnswer: The Mishnah (Sotah 7:1) does indeed permit the Shema, the Amidah and Birkat Hamazon in any language one understands, and it is better to pray with understanding than without it. But Hebrew is the language of the Torah and the language in which the whole Jewish people prays; the text of the prayers was composed by the sages with deep meaning in every word, and a translation inevitably loses some of it. Praying in Hebrew unites me with the community in any synagogue in the world. That is why I learn at least the main prayers — the Shema, the Amidah, the blessings — in Hebrew, and read the translation so that I understand them.

questions.prompt: Why should an adult, a candidate for giyur, learn the Hebrew alphabet? Tell us how you yourself are learning the letters.
questions.modelAnswer: The beit din usually does not require me to be fluent in the language, but it does expect that I can read the prayers, at least slowly, and know the key words. The letters open up the text of the siddur itself: this way I can follow the cantor and find the right place, keeping the translation alongside. The alphabet has 22 letters, it is read from right to left, there are no capital letters, and five letters change their form at the end of a word. I learn it in groups: every day I repeat aloud the names of one group, and then I look for those letters in the headings of the siddur. Usually after two or three weeks of fifteen-minute sessions the letters stop being “pictures”.
keyPoints: The beit din usually expects slow reading of the prayers, not fluency in the language

questions.prompt: Read the word בָּרוּךְ aloud and tell us everything you know about it.
questions.modelAnswer: I read from right to left: “ba-ruch”, “blessed”. בָּ is bet with a dagesh and a kamatz, that is, “ba”; ר is resh; וּ is vav with a dot in the middle, the vowel “u” (shuruk), not the consonant “v”; ךְ is final chaf, one of the five final forms, which are remembered by the word “MaNTzePaCh”. By tradition a shva is written under the final chaf, but at the end of a word it is not pronounced, so the word is read “baruch”, with no vowel after the “ch”. This word opens the formula of a blessing, “Baruch atah Adonai…”, and I say it many times a day.
keyPoints: The order of the letters from right to left: בָּ + ר + וּ + ךְ

questions.prompt: What are nekudot, and why are they needed if the letters are already there? How do you practice reading with vowel points?
questions.modelAnswer: Hebrew letters represent only consonants, while the vowels are marked by small signs — nekudot; this system was set down in Tiberias in the 7th–10th centuries by the Masoretes, preserving the reading that had been passed down orally. I read syllable by syllable: first a letter with its vowel, and only then the next letter. Every day I read aloud one short line from the siddur, for example “Baruch atah Adonai Eloheinu melech ha'olam”, until it becomes familiar. Slow reading is not a failure: even experienced worshippers read an unfamiliar text syllable by syllable.
keyPoints: Nekudot are vowel signs; the system was set down in the 7th–10th centuries by the Masoretes of Tiberias

questions.prompt: Which pronunciation is customary in your community — Ashkenazi or Israeli? Why do you keep to it?
questions.modelAnswer: Both pronunciations are legitimate: the Ashkenazi one, heard in many synagogues of the diaspora, and the Israeli one, which is Sephardi in origin. The same signs are read differently: in Ashkenazi pronunciation kamatz sounds like “o” (“boruch” instead of “baruch”), cholam most often like “oy” (“Toyre”, “sholoym”; in the Lithuanian tradition like “ey”), and tav without a dagesh like “s” (“Shabbos” instead of “Shabbat”). In Israeli pronunciation the same words sound “baruch”, “Torah”, “shalom”, “Shabbat”. I keep to one pronunciation — the one customary in my community — and pray the way it does.

questions.prompt: What do the words “Ve'ahavta” — “and you shall love Hashem with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your means” — mean to you? How does this show itself in your life?
questions.modelAnswer: “Ve'ahavta” is Devarim 6:5, the continuation of the Shema, and for me these words are where the program of Jewish life begins. The sages interpret the three measures of love this way: “with all your heart” — with both inclinations, the good and the evil, that is, with your whole nature; “with all your soul” — even if you must give up your life; “with all your means” — with all your possessions and all your strength. From the verses that follow come the study of Torah, teaching children, tefillin and mezuzah: love of G-d takes shape in concrete mitzvot. I try to read the Shema morning and evening — “when you lie down and when you rise up” — to study Torah, and to build a home where these words do not remain just a text.
