questions.explanation: The alphabet is called alef-bet after its first two letters, just as the name “alpha-beta” is made up of the first Greek letters.

questions.prompt: Which letter is the smallest and begins the word “Yisrael”?
options: Vav — the letter “v”
Yud — the letter “y”
Zayin — the letter “z”
Dalet — the letter “d”
questions.explanation: Yud is almost a dot, the smallest letter; יִשְׂרָאֵל begins with it, and tradition calls it a symbol of humility.

questions.prompt: Why does Russian transcription write “Rosh a-Shana”, even though in Hebrew there is the letter hei there?
options: In this name hei is read as “sh”
Hei at the start of a word always gives an “r” sound
Hei is a light breath, and in writing it is often lost
Hei here simply replaces the letter shin
questions.explanation: Hei is a light breath; in Russian transcription it is often lost, hence “Rosh a-Shana” and “a-motzi”.

questions.prompt: What is the gematria of the word “chai” (“alive”), and which letters give it?
options: Ten: the letter yud on its own
Twenty-six: dalet and vav
Thirty-six: lamed and vav
Eighteen: chet — 8 and yud — 10
questions.explanation: Chet equals 8, yud equals 10; together 18, which is why on festive occasions people give gifts in multiples of eighteen.

questions.prompt: Which year from the creation of the world does the lesson write with the letters תשפ״ז?
options: The year 5785, and the thousands must be written
The year 5787, the thousands are usually omitted
The year 5700, the hundreds are not included
The year 5870, the letters are read left to right
questions.explanation: The lesson gives this very example: תשפ״ז is the year 5787 from the creation of the world, and in this kind of notation the thousands are usually omitted.

questions.prompt: Hebrew writing has no capital letters.
questions.explanation: There are no capital letters; only five letters have a special form, and only at the end of a word.

questions.prompt: A final kaf with a dagesh inside is the usual form at the end of a word.
questions.explanation: Final chaf is almost always written with the two dots of a shva; a final kaf with a dot is extremely rare.

questions.prompt: Match each letter with a distinguishing feature of its shape.
pairs: A sharp corner with a projection
questions.explanation: Similar letters are told apart by corner, rounding and tail; lamed is the only one that rises above the line.

questions.prompt: What mnemonic word helps you remember the five letters that have a final form?
questions.explanation: The traditional mnemonic for the five final letters is “MaNTzePaCh” (מנצפ״ך): mem, nun, tzadi, pei, kaf.

questions.prompt: The beit din asks: why do you need to tell apart the printed type of the siddur and handwritten cursive?
questions.modelAnswer: In the Torah, the siddur and books I see the printed square script, ktav ashuri, and that is the one I am learning, so that I can follow the service and find my place in the prayer book. For handwriting there is a cursive script, and its letters look different, so I do not expect a note to look like a page of the siddur. The beit din usually does not require fluency in the language from me: it is enough to read the prayers slowly and know the key words. So I reinforce the square letters and look for them in the headings of the siddur.
keyPoints: Ktav ashuri is the square script of the Torah and the siddur
Cursive for handwriting looks different
For the beit din, slow reading of the prayers is what matters
Practice: looking for letters in the headings of the siddur
questions.explanation: The lesson distinguishes ktav ashuri in the Torah and siddur from the cursive of everyday writing, and connects reading the letters with being able to follow the service.

questions.prompt: Explain to the beit din why the same sound in Hebrew is often written with different letters.
questions.modelAnswer: The sounds “k”, “t”, “s”, “v” and “ch” can each be represented by two letters. “K” is written with kaf with a dagesh and with kuf, “t” with tet and tav, “s” with samech and sin, “v” with bet without a dot and vav, “ch” with chet and chaf. In ancient times these letters sounded different, but today the distinction survives mainly in spelling. So when I hear a word I cannot always say right away how it is spelled, and the spelling has to be memorized. For prayer it matters to me to recognize the letters in the siddur, not just to repeat the sound by ear.
keyPoints: Pairs of letters for the sounds k, t, s, v and ch
In ancient times these letters were pronounced differently
Today the difference is mainly in spelling
Spelling is memorized separately from hearing
questions.explanation: The lesson lists the pairs of letters that share the same sounds today and says that the ancient distinction has survived mainly in spelling.

questions.prompt: Where is full vocalization printed so that you can learn to read with it?
options: On the Torah scroll in the aron hakodesh
In a newspaper line without a single dot
In the siddur, the Chumash and children's books
Only in the handwritten cursive of letters
questions.explanation: The Torah scroll is written without vowel points, while the siddur, the Chumash and children's books are printed with full vocalization — and that is what people learn from.
questions.source: Lesson: Vowel Points (Nekudot) and Reading Syllables

questions.prompt: In which syllable does even the Israeli reading give kamatz an “o” sound?
options: In any stressed open syllable
Only under the guttural letter alef
Only at the very end of a word
In a closed unstressed one — this is kamatz katan
questions.explanation: Kamatz katan, the “small kamatz”, sounds like “o” in a closed unstressed syllable: כָּל — “kol”, חָכְמָה — “chochmah”.
questions.source: Lesson: Vowel Points (Nekudot) and Reading Syllables

questions.prompt: How is the word רוּחַ read, and what happens to the vowel under the last letter?
options: “Ruach”: a hidden patach sounds before the chet
“Rucha”: patach always comes after the consonant
“Rauch”: the shuruk in this word is silent
“Reach”: a cholam replaces the final patach
questions.explanation: If a word ends in chet or ayin with a patach, the patach genuvah is pronounced before the consonant: רוּחַ is “ruach”, not “rucha”.
questions.source: Lesson: Vowel Points (Nekudot) and Reading Syllables

questions.prompt: Which letters, as a rule, do not take a dagesh?
options: Bet, kaf and pei at the start of a word
The gutturals alef, hei, chet, ayin and resh
Only the five final sofit forms
Only tav and gimel after a shva
questions.explanation: The gutturals alef, hei, chet and ayin usually do not take a dagesh and get a chataf instead of a simple shva; resh, as a rule, also has no dagesh.
questions.source: Lesson: Vowel Points (Nekudot) and Reading Syllables

questions.prompt: In Israeli pronunciation kamatz and patach give the same sound, “a”.
questions.explanation: In Israeli pronunciation both kamatz and patach are read as “a”; kamatz as “o” is a mark of Ashkenazi reading, except for kamatz katan.
questions.source: Lesson: Vowel Points (Nekudot) and Reading Syllables

questions.prompt: A shva at the end of a word is always pronounced as the vowel “e”.
questions.explanation: At the end of a word a shva is always silent; under final chaf it is written by tradition, but “baruch” is read with no vowel after the “ch”.
questions.source: Lesson: Vowel Points (Nekudot) and Reading Syllables

questions.prompt: The chataf segol under the alef in the word “Eloheinu” gives a very short “e”.
questions.explanation: In the word אֱלֹהֵינוּ there is a chataf segol under the alef, a very short “e”, and the word is read “E-lo-hei-nu”.
questions.source: Lesson: Vowel Points (Nekudot) and Reading Syllables

questions.prompt: Match each vowel sign with how it looks in writing.
pairs: Three slanting dots under the letter
questions.explanation: Kamatz looks like a small “T”, patach is a line, tzere is two dots, segol is a triangle, kubutz is three slanting dots.
questions.source: Lesson: Vowel Points (Nekudot) and Reading Syllables

questions.prompt: What is writing without vowel points called, where vav and yud hint at the vowels?
questions.explanation: In newspapers and on signs vav indicates “o” or “u”, and yud indicates “i” or “e”; this kind of writing is called “ktiv male”, full spelling.
questions.source: Lesson: Vowel Points (Nekudot) and Reading Syllables

questions.prompt: At the beit din you are asked to explain the shva: when is it pronounced, and when is it silent?
questions.modelAnswer: A shva is two dots, one above the other, under a letter. Shva na, the mobile shva, I pronounce as a short “e”: at the start of a word, under the second of two letters with shva in a row, and under a letter with a strengthening dagesh. Shva nach, the resting shva, is silent and simply closes the syllable, like the shva under the sin in the word “Yisrael”. At the end of a word a shva is always silent, even though under final chaf it is written by tradition, and “baruch” does not get an extra vowel. This way I do not add an “e” where the syllable is already closed.
keyPoints: Shva na — a short “e” at the start of a word and in two special cases
Shva nach is silent and closes the syllable
At the end of a word the shva is not pronounced
Under final chaf the dots are written by tradition
questions.explanation: The lesson divides the shva into mobile and resting, and names three cases in which shva na is pronounced, while at the end of a word it is silent.
questions.source: Lesson: Vowel Points (Nekudot) and Reading Syllables

questions.prompt: The beit din asks: where does the stress usually fall in Hebrew, and what is special about segolate words?
questions.modelAnswer: I read most words with the stress on the last syllable: shaLOM, toRAH, mitzVAH. Segolate words keep the stress on the second-to-last syllable, and the lesson names “MElech” and “Eretz”. If I put the stress in the wrong place, the word sounds foreign, even though the letters are the same. In the Tanakh the stress is marked by the cantillation signs, te'amim, and in the siddur there is sometimes a small vertical line. While I am learning, I check the stress against the reading of my community and do not rush.
keyPoints: The usual stress is on the last syllable
Segolate words — on the second-to-last: melech, eretz
In the Tanakh the stress is marked by te'amim
In the siddur there is sometimes a small line
questions.explanation: The lesson says the stress is most often on the last syllable, while in segolate words like “melech” and “eretz” it is on the second-to-last, and it mentions te'amim.
questions.source: Lesson: Vowel Points (Nekudot) and Reading Syllables

questions.prompt: How does the Shema differ from a request addressed to the Almighty?
options: It is read only by kohanim on Yom Kippur
It replaces the Amidah at weekday Minchah
It is said only once, before giyur
It is a declaration of unity, not a request
questions.explanation: “Shema Yisrael” is the central declaration of faith: the Almighty is the G-d of Israel, and He is One; it is not a prayer of request.

questions.prompt: What do you do with your right hand while saying the first verse of the Shema?
options: Cover your eyes with it so as not to be distracted
Point with it toward the aron hakodesh
Touch the mezuzah and kiss your fingers
Raise it while answering “Barechu”
questions.explanation: During the first verse it is customary to cover your eyes with your right hand and draw out the word “echad”, without being distracted by anything.

questions.prompt: How many blessings surround the full reading of the Shema in the morning and in the evening?
options: In the morning one before and one after, the same in the evening
In the morning three before the Shema, no berachot in the evening
In the morning two before and one after, in the evening two before and two after
Morning and evening, only a whispered “Baruch shem”
questions.explanation: The full Shema includes three passages and the berachot around them: in the morning two before and one after, in the evening two before and two after.

questions.prompt: What is required for the first verse of the Shema to count as fulfilling the mitzvah?
options: It is enough to run your eyes over the verse silently
Kavanah: without thought for the meaning, the mitzvah is not fulfilled
A minyan of ten adult men is needed
The verse is read only standing and only in Hebrew
questions.explanation: The first verse is said with kavanah: if a person said it without thinking about its meaning, they have not fulfilled the mitzvah.

questions.prompt: “Baruch shem” was first said by the Kohen Gadol (high priest) — in response to the Shema of Yaakov's sons.
questions.explanation: According to the Talmud (Pesachim 56a), it was Yaakov himself who answered “Baruch shem”; in the Temple this line was said when the Kohen Gadol pronounced the Name.

questions.prompt: It is preferable to read the evening Shema before midnight, and if necessary it may be read until dawn.
questions.explanation: The evening Shema is read after the stars come out; preferably before midnight, and if necessary until dawn.

questions.prompt: Match each word of the first verse of the Shema with the meaning the lesson gives it.
pairs: Not only to listen, but to accept
The whole people and each individual
Our G-d, the G-d of Israel
questions.explanation: The lesson goes through the verse word by word: “shema” — accept, “Yisrael” — the people and each individual, “Eloheinu” — our G-d, “echad” — One.

questions.prompt: What is the reading of the Shema said before going to sleep called?
questions.explanation: Before sleep one reads the “Shema al hamitah”, at least the first passage, together with the blessing “HaMapil”.

questions.prompt: The beit din asks: in what order do the three passages of the Shema come, and why does the Mishnah place them this way?
questions.modelAnswer: First I accept upon myself the sovereignty of Heaven: this is “Shema” and “Ve'ahavta”, Devarim 6:4–9, about the unity of G-d and love for Him. Then comes “Vehayah im shamoa”, Devarim 11:13–21: here I accept the yoke of the mitzvot and hear about reward and responsibility. The third passage, “Vayomer”, Bamidbar 15:37–41, reminds us of tzitzit and of the Exodus from Egypt. The Mishnah in Berachot 2:2 explains the order this way: first the sovereignty of Heaven, then the mitzvot. So when I learn the whole Shema, I do not rearrange the passages.
keyPoints: First the yoke of the Kingdom of Heaven, Devarim 6:4–9
Then the yoke of the mitzvot, Devarim 11:13–21
The third passage — tzitzit and the Exodus
The order is explained by Mishnah Berachot 2:2
questions.explanation: Mishnah Berachot 2:2 places accepting the sovereignty of Heaven before accepting the mitzvot, and the lesson names the three passages in this order.

differs.text: In Reform siddurim the second passage (Devarim 11:13–21) was traditionally omitted or replaced; in “Mishkan T'filah” it is given as an option.

questions.prompt: Whom does halacha obligate to read the Shema morning and evening, and what is customary for those who are exempt from this obligation?
questions.modelAnswer: According to halacha, as the lesson presents it, men are obligated to read the Shema morning and evening. Women are exempt from the Shema as a time-bound mitzvah, but it is customary for them to say at least the first verse. I take the first verse seriously: it is said with kavanah, and without thought for its meaning the mitzvah is not fulfilled. I pronounce the words clearly and do not run the end of one word into the beginning of the next. That way the Shema remains a testimony, not a patter.
keyPoints: Men are obligated to recite the Shema morning and evening
Women are exempt, as it is a time-bound mitzvah
It is customary for women to say the first verse
Kavanah and clear pronunciation are required
questions.explanation: The Orthodox section of the lesson obligates men to recite the Shema morning and evening, and says of women that it is customary to say at least the first verse.

questions.prompt: What does the Talmud call the Amidah when it simply speaks of “prayer”?
options: HaTefillah — “the Prayer” without further qualification
Ashrei — the psalm at the start of Minchah
Kedushah — the congregation's response “Holy”
Musaf — an addition to the weekday service
questions.explanation: In the Talmud the Amidah is called “HaTefillah”: when the Sages speak of “prayer” without further qualification, it is the Amidah they mean.
questions.source: Lesson: The Amidah and the three daily prayers

questions.prompt: Which of the three daily prayers is the shortest in content?
options: Shacharit: it has psalms, the Shema and the Amidah
Maariv: the Shema is recited twice in a row
Minchah: Ashrei, the Amidah and the closing prayers
Neilah: it is recited every weekday evening
questions.explanation: Minchah is the afternoon prayer, said from after midday until sunset; the lesson calls it the shortest: Ashrei, the Amidah and the closing prayers.
questions.source: Lesson: The Amidah and the three daily prayers

questions.prompt: Which prayer is added on Yom Kippur beyond Shacharit, Minchah, Maariv and Musaf?
options: Ashrei in place of the evening Shema
Birkat HaMazon right after Musaf
The whole congregation repeating “Modeh Ani”
Neilah — the prayer of the “closing of the gates”
questions.explanation: On Yom Kippur there is a fifth prayer — Neilah, the “closing of the gates”; Musaf, by contrast, is added on Shabbat, festivals and Rosh Chodesh.
questions.source: Lesson: The Amidah and the three daily prayers

questions.prompt: According to the Talmud, who arranged the text of the Amidah at the start of the Second Temple era?
options: The Patriarchs Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov
The Men of the Great Assembly
Rabbi Akiva at the hour of his death
The High Priest on the day of Yom Kippur
questions.explanation: The Talmud (Megillah 17b) says that the text of the Amidah was arranged by the Men of the Great Assembly at the start of the Second Temple era.

questions.prompt: By when is it best to say the morning Amidah, and what deadline is still acceptable?
options: Ideally by the end of the fourth hour; the latest is midday
Only until sunrise; after that it is no longer valid
Until the stars come out, the same deadline as the evening Shema
Until the end of the third hour, the same deadline as the Shema
questions.explanation: It is best to say the morning Amidah by the end of the fourth hour of the day, although if necessary it may be said until midday.

questions.prompt: On Shabbat, the middle part of the Amidah is filled with the same thirteen requests as on weekdays.
questions.explanation: On Shabbat and festivals we do not ask for our weekday needs: the middle requests are replaced by a single blessing about the holiness of the day.
questions.source: Lesson: The Amidah and the three daily prayers

questions.prompt: Before the Amidah one takes three steps back and three steps forward, and at the end three steps back.
questions.explanation: Three steps back and three forward before beginning are like approaching the King, and three steps back at the end are taking leave.
questions.source: Lesson: The Amidah and the three daily prayers

questions.prompt: Match each blessing of the weekday Amidah with its theme.
pairs: Thanksgiving for the miracles of every day
The Temple service and the return of the Shechinah to Zion
A request that our prayer be heard
questions.explanation: The lesson calls Gevurot the second blessing, Avodah, Modim and Shalom the last three, and “Who hears prayer” the sixteenth.
questions.source: Lesson: The Amidah and the three daily prayers

questions.prompt: What is the name of the aloud repetition of the Amidah that the shaliach tzibbur leads after the silent prayer?
questions.explanation: After the silent Amidah, the shaliach tzibbur repeats it aloud — this is chazarat hashatz, and the congregation answers “amen”.

questions.prompt: From which word of the Torah do the Sages derive that ten people are needed for a “matter of holiness”?
questions.explanation: The number ten is derived from the word “congregation” (edah), which the Torah used for the ten spies.

questions.prompt: The beit din asks: which way do you face during the Amidah, and whose example set its whisper?
questions.modelAnswer: I pray the Amidah standing, facing toward Jerusalem, and if I were in Jerusalem itself, facing the Temple Mount. The Sages took the quiet voice from Channah, the mother of the prophet Shmuel: she spoke in her heart, her lips moved, but her voice was not heard. That is how I pray too — so that only I myself hear the words. This is not a whisper out of uncertainty, but a way of standing before the King. I can add my own request in the blessing “Who hears prayer” and in a personal prayer at the end, in any language.
keyPoints: Facing Jerusalem; in Jerusalem, facing the Temple Mount
The model of silence is Channah, Shmuel I 1:13
The lips move, but no voice is heard
Personal words are allowed in “Who hears prayer” and at the end
questions.explanation: The lesson instructs us to pray facing Jerusalem, following the example of Channah's silent prayer, and allows our own words in “Who hears prayer” and at the end of the Amidah.

questions.prompt: What must be said in a berachah, or else it is not considered complete?
options: The name of the person praying and of their community
The word “amen”, with which the formula ends
G-d's Name and His Kingship — “melech ha'olam”
The names of Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov in a row
questions.explanation: The words “King of the universe” are essential: a blessing without mention of the Name and Kingship is not considered complete.

questions.prompt: Which berachah is said when washing the hands from a vessel before a meal with bread?
options: “Shehecheyanu” — for the joy of a new day
“Borei pri ha'adamah” — over the water itself
“HaMotzi” — over the water used for washing
“Al netilat yadayim” — on washing the hands
questions.explanation: Before eating bread, the hands are washed from a vessel and one says “…al netilat yadayim” after the words “asher kidshanu… vetzivanu”.

questions.prompt: According to tradition, who composed the first three blessings of Birkat HaMazon?
options: Moshe — food, Yehoshua — the Land, David and Shlomo — Jerusalem
Avraham — bread, Yitzchak — wine, Yaakov — the end of the meal
Rabbi Meir — three berachot, the High Priest — the fourth
Channah — food, Daniel — the Land, David — only peace
questions.explanation: According to tradition, Moshe composed the first berachah, Yehoshua the second, and David and Shlomo the third; the fourth, “Who is good and does good”, was added in Yavneh.

questions.prompt: How often does a sofer check a home mezuzah, and why?
options: Every month, because the case is replaced
Twice in seven years: the letters may become damaged
Only on moving-in day, and only in Israel
Once every eighteen years, by the number “chai”
questions.explanation: A sofer checks the mezuzah at home twice in seven years, since the letters on the parchment may become damaged.

questions.prompt: If a meal began with bread, separate berachot are usually not said over the other dishes.
questions.explanation: The blessing “HaMotzi” covers the whole meal: after it, separate berachot are usually not said over the other dishes.

questions.prompt: “Shehakol” is chosen in advance for any food, even when the correct berachah is known.
questions.explanation: If a person is in doubt, “shehakol” counts after the fact for any food, but one should not do this in advance.

questions.prompt: Match each thanksgiving after eating with the situation from the lesson.
pairs: Food that did not include bread
“Who is good and does good”, from Yavneh
questions.explanation: After bread — Birkat HaMazon; with three adults — zimun; after other food — the short berachot; the fourth berachah was added in Yavneh.

questions.prompt: How does a woman say the first morning words of thanks for the soul restored to her?
questions.explanation: A woman says “Modah ani”; G-d's Name does not appear in these words, so they are said immediately upon waking, even before washing the hands.

questions.prompt: At what moment do you say “Shehecheyanu”, and what does this berachah give thanks for?
questions.modelAnswer: I say “Shehecheyanu” over something new and joyful: the Almighty has given us life, sustained us and allowed us to reach this time. According to the Mishnah, it is said when a person has built a new house or bought new things. By custom, I say it at the start of a festival — at kiddush and at candle lighting — on the first night of Chanukah, over the first fruit of the season, and over important new clothing. On the day of giyur many say it after immersing in the mikveh, although community customs differ here, and I will ask what is done in ours. For me it is thanks not for the thing itself, but for having lived to reach this moment.
keyPoints: Thanks for life and for having reached this time
Mishnah: a new house or new things
Custom: festivals, the first night of Chanukah, a new fruit, clothing
On the day of giyur, community customs differ
questions.explanation: Mishnah Berachot 9:3 links “Shehecheyanu” with a new house and new things, and the lesson adds festivals, Chanukah, a new fruit and the differing customs of the day of giyur.

differs.text: In Reform communities “Shehecheyanu” is said with the same formula, but observing berachot is a matter of personal choice rather than a halachic obligation.

questions.prompt: Outside Israel, within what time is a mezuzah put up in rented housing, and on which doorways is it not placed?
questions.modelAnswer: Outside Israel, if the home is rented, the mezuzah may be put up within thirty days of moving in. It is not placed on a bathroom or toilet: a mezuzah is needed on the doorways of living rooms. Inside there must be a kosher parchment handwritten by a sofer; a purchased case without such a parchment is not yet a mezuzah. Over time the letters deteriorate, so a sofer checks a home mezuzah twice in seven years. For me, the moving-in deadline and the checking are part of the mitzvah itself, not a small detail to leave “for later”.
keyPoints: Outside Israel, in rented housing — within 30 days
Not placed on a bathroom or toilet
A handwritten kosher parchment is needed, not an empty case
Checked by a sofer twice in seven years
questions.explanation: The Orthodox section gives thirty days for rented housing outside Israel, excludes the bathroom and toilet, and instructs that the mezuzah be checked twice in seven years.

questions.prompt: Which lamp in the synagogue recalls the menorah of the Temple?
options: Candles placed on the bimah
A chanukiah by the front door
A lamp above the hall's partition
Ner tamid — the eternal light
questions.explanation: The ner tamid is the eternal light in the synagogue, lit in memory of the Temple menorah.
questions.source: Lesson: The siddur, the synagogue, tallit, tefillin and kippah

questions.prompt: How does Nusach Sefard differ from Nusach Edot HaMizrach?
options: Sefard — Eastern communities; Edot HaMizrach — Chasidim
Sefard — the Chasidic nusach; Edot HaMizrach — Sephardim and the East
Both nusachim omit both the Shema and the Amidah
Edot HaMizrach pray only from a machzor
questions.explanation: Nusach Sefard is used by Chasidim and is connected with the Kabbalists; Nusach Edot HaMizrach is used by Sephardi and Eastern communities. Both include the Shema and the Amidah.
questions.source: Lesson: The siddur, the synagogue, tallit, tefillin and kippah

questions.prompt: How many windings between the knots of tzitzit do Ashkenazim make?
options: Five, five, five and five
Ten, ten, ten and ten
Seven, eight, eleven and thirteen
Four, four, four and four
questions.explanation: Between the five double knots, Ashkenazim make 7, 8, 11 and 13 windings; the strings themselves are four, folded in half.

questions.prompt: How many blessings over tefillin do Ashkenazim say, and how many do Sephardim say?
options: Ashkenazim — two; Sephardim — one, on the arm
Ashkenazim — one; Sephardim — two, on the head
Both say three, counting the strap
Only the sofer says one, when writing the parchment
questions.explanation: Ashkenazim say “lehaniach tefillin” over the arm tefillin and “al mitzvat tefillin” over the head tefillin; Sephardim say one blessing, over the arm tefillin.

questions.prompt: The synagogue replaces the Temple, which is why it is called the great Sanctuary.
questions.explanation: The synagogue does not replace the Temple; the Sages call it a “small Sanctuary”, mikdash me'at.
questions.source: Lesson: The siddur, the synagogue, tallit, tefillin and kippah

questions.prompt: All Jews begin wearing the large tallit only after their wedding.
questions.explanation: Many Ashkenazim from Poland and Lithuania put on the large tallit after the wedding, while Sephardim and German Jews do so from bar mitzvah.

questions.prompt: The strap of the arm tefillin is wound around the forearm seven times.
questions.explanation: The strap of the arm tefillin is wound around the forearm seven times: Ashkenazim wind it outward, Sephardim and Chasidim inward.

questions.prompt: Match the words of prayer with what they refer to.
pairs: The berachah said when wrapping oneself in the tallit
The berachah on putting on tefillin
The verse said on entering the synagogue
The synagogue as a small Sanctuary
questions.explanation: “Lehitatef batzitzit” is said over the tallit, “lehaniach tefillin” over tefillin, “Mah tovu” on entering, and mikdash me'at is the Sages' name for the synagogue.
questions.source: Lesson: The siddur, the synagogue, tallit, tefillin and kippah

questions.prompt: What is the women's gallery in an Orthodox synagogue called?
questions.explanation: Women may sit in a separate gallery, the ezrat nashim; another way of separating is a partition, the mechitzah.
questions.source: Lesson: The siddur, the synagogue, tallit, tefillin and kippah

questions.prompt: The beit din asks: is the kippah a mitzvah of the Torah? Why do you cover your head?
questions.modelAnswer: For me the kippah is not a mitzvah of the Torah, but an ancient custom of awe before Heaven. The Talmud tells of a sage who would not walk even four cubits with his head uncovered, because “the Shechinah is above me”. In the synagogue the head is covered in all movements, and I do as is customary in my community. The color and material of a kippah may show which community a person feels close to, but they have no halachic significance. A covered head reminds me before Whom I stand, even before I open the siddur.
keyPoints: The kippah is a custom, not a mitzvah of the Torah
“The Shechinah is above me”: not walking four cubits with an uncovered head
In the synagogue the head is covered in all movements
Color and material are not halachically important
questions.explanation: The lesson states plainly that the kippah is not a mitzvah of the Torah, and cites the story from Kiddushin 31a about awe before the Shechinah.

questions.prompt: Which teaching about G-d is, for Judaism, a false teaching (minut)?
options: That the Almighty is One and His unity is unlike any other
That the Almighty has no body and no form
That the Almighty consists of several “persons” or becomes a human being
That the first verse of the Shema proclaims G-d's unity
questions.explanation: The Almighty is One and indivisible, without body or form; a teaching of G-d in several persons is, for Judaism, a false teaching.
questions.source: Devarim 6:4; Bamidbar 23:19; Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 1:7–8

questions.prompt: To whom is prayer addressed in the Amidah, according to Judaism?
options: To an angel, so that it passes the request on to G-d
Only to the Almighty, directly and without an intermediary
To a holy person as an intercessor
To an image, as long as the heart is turned to G-d
questions.explanation: We pray only to the Creator, without an intermediary: not to an angel, not to a human being, not to a saint and not to an image. The Rambam makes this the fifth principle and counts one who sets up an intermediary among the minim (Laws of Teshuvah 3:7).
questions.source: Rambam, the 5th of the 13 principles; Laws of Teshuvah 3:7

questions.prompt: Where in the weekday Amidah do we say “for Your salvation we hope all day long”?
options: In the tenth blessing, on the ingathering of the exiles
In the thirteenth blessing, on the righteous and the gerim
In the fourteenth, on Jerusalem and the throne of David
In the fifteenth, “Et tzemach David”
questions.explanation: These words — “ki lishuatcha kivinu kol hayom” — are in the fifteenth blessing. The salvation is still ahead: Mashiach has not come.

questions.prompt: Which siddur has been the main prayer book of the North American Reform movement since 2007?
options: Mishkan T'filah
Siddur Tehillat Hashem
Kitzur Shulchan Aruch
Sefer Yetzirah
questions.explanation: Mishkan T'filah (CCAR Press, 2007) replaced the 1975 Gates of Prayer. In Russian-speaking communities the siddur may be different.

questions.prompt: What is characteristic of many Reform siddurim in the text of the Amidah?
options: Alongside the Patriarchs, the Matriarchs are named: Sarah, Rivka, Rachel and Leah
The Amidah is entirely replaced by a single psalm in the community's language
G-d's Name is neither said nor written in the Amidah, even in the siddur
The Amidah is recited only by men over sixty years of age
questions.explanation: Including the Imahot emphasizes equality in the covenant; the exact wording depends on the edition.
questions.source: Mishkan T'filah; lesson on the siddur

questions.prompt: In Reform Judaism, prayer in an understandable language is a deliberate principle: a person should understand what they are saying to the Almighty, while Hebrew remains the sacred language of the people.
questions.explanation: This is not a replacement of Hebrew and not a “concession”, but a principle of understanding, alongside which communities teach the Hebrew text.
questions.source: Lesson “The siddur, the synagogue, tallit, tefillin and kippah”

questions.prompt: What is the name of the Reform machzor for the Days of Awe, published by the CCAR as a companion to the siddur Mishkan T'filah?
questions.explanation: Mishkan HaNefesh is the machzor for the Days of Awe of the North American progressive movement.

questions.prompt: According to the Rambam, what does the word *echad* in the Shema express?
options: A unity that can be made up of several “persons”
A unity unlike any other: G-d is not made up of parts
That G-d became a human being and remained one
The unity of the people, not of G-d
questions.explanation: The Rambam (Foundations of the Torah 1:7) reads echad as a unity without parts or “persons”.
questions.source: Devarim 6:4; Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 1:7

questions.prompt: In the Amidah one may turn to a tzaddik or an angel as an intermediary between a person and G-d.
questions.explanation: We pray only to the Almighty, directly and without an intermediary (Rambam, 5th principle).

questions.prompt: What should you check when choosing a new synagogue?
options: Only how beautiful the kippot and melodies are
Recognition of the community by a known movement, and its teaching about G-d, Mashiach and the Torah
Only whether the holiday services are free of charge
Whether a Hebrew name is enough
questions.explanation: Outward signs are no substitute for checking the teaching and the affiliation with a known movement.
questions.source: Lesson: The siddur, the synagogue, tallit, tefillin and kippah

questions.prompt: Which way do you face when saying the Amidah?
options: Toward the sunrise, wherever you stand
Toward Jerusalem
Toward the community's teacher
Toward any wall, as long as it is made of stone
questions.explanation: The Amidah is said standing, facing Jerusalem — the eternal capital and the direction of Jewish prayer.
